title: Ang 10–12: So Purakh
hook: the Rehras hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan
tomorrow: why do the night prayers come before the first raga?

segments.voice: Last time, ang eight: the Japji's last salok, then So Dar on the same page. Morning meets evening. Now the evening goes on, in a new voice.

Dusk at a truck stop off the interstate. Engines idling, the sky going orange over the pumps. A driver props his phone against the steering wheel. It's his turn in the family's reading, and he's doing it from a few states away. He scrolls past So Dar and slows down. The heading has changed: Mahala 4. The hymn opens, so purakh niranjan, and he reads to the end of the verse. The name there is Nanak. But the heading says four. So who's speaking?
screen: `DUSK AT A TRUCK STOP.` → `HIS TURN IN THE FAMILY'S READING.` → `MAHALA 4, SIGNED NANAK?`

segments.voice: Mahala 4 means the fourth Guru: Guru Ram Das. Here's the thing to tell someone tonight. The Gurus who came after Guru Nanak signed their hymns with his name, Nanak. So the name in the verse stays the same, and the heading's number tells you whose voice it is. Sikhs say the same light passed from Guru to Guru, and the shared name fits that. Now the hymn itself. So purakh niranjan: that Being, spotless, without a stain. In paraphrase, the hymn goes on: all meditate on You, true Creator; every being is Yours, and You give to every being. These are the So Purakh hymns, part of the Rehras, the evening prayer. Then, on ang twelve, the heading changes again: Mahala 5, Guru Arjan. And a line that lands at dusk, in the original: gobind milan kee eh teree bareeaa. This is your turn to meet the Lord of the universe. So in a few evening pages, three Gurus speak, one name runs through them, and the last word is about now. The driver at the pump keeps reading.
screen: `MAHALA 4: GURU RAM DAS.` · `ONE NAME, MANY VOICES: NANAK.` · `SO PURAKH NIRANJAN: SPOTLESS.` · `MAHALA 5: THIS IS YOUR TURN.` · then, large: `THE EVENING PAGES.`

segments.voice: If you can, open to ang ten and read the first line, so purakh niranjan, once. Then close your eyes and let the day settle, the way the sky settles at dusk. When a thought from today comes up, set it down beside you and come back to the breath.
Ang 10. Where So Purakh begins: the evening pages, in the voice of the fourth Guru. Today's word.
For the road: the evening pages, where many voices sign the one name. Sleep well tonight.

howItsDone: Sikhs say the Rehras at dusk, at home or in the gurdwara; in the Guru Granth Sahib its hymns begin with So Dar on ang 8 and continue with So Purakh, by Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, on angs 10 to 12.

Surprising fact: the Gurus after Guru Nanak signed their hymns as Nanak; the heading's mahala number names the Guru. Taught in passing on day 1432 (Reading the heading); here it is the story's answer. 'Sikhs say the same light passed from Guru to Guru': confirm phrasing.

So Purakh (Asa M4, Ang 10–11) paraphrased after the opening words; Asa M5 on Ang 12 quoted in transliteration of the original ('gobind milan kee eh teree bareeaa', as in this path's day 412). Confirm.

'In a few evening pages, three Gurus speak' counts Guru Nanak (So Dar), Guru Ram Das (So Purakh) and Guru Arjan (Ang 12); So Dar also includes hymns of other Gurus. Confirm the phrasing is not misleading.
